sections.heading: Fabrication and performance of Tile transducers for piezoelectric energy harvesting
sections.text:
Cite as: AIP Advances 10, 045326 (2020); doi: 10.1063/5.0002400 Submitted: 28 January 2020 $\bullet$ Accepted: 20 March 2020 • Published Online: 16 April 2020

Zhiming Liu,1 Guangya Ding,1 Jun Wang,1,a) Guojun Cai,2 Xiangzhen Qin,1 and Kaixi Shi1

sections.heading: AFFILIATIONS
ABSTRACT
sections.text:
In recent years, pavement piezoelectric energy harvesting has become one of the most promising road energy harvesting system clean energy sources. However, it is difficult for existing piezoelectric transducer structures to meet road power generation requirements. In this study, ceramic grinding and polishing techniques were used to make curved piezoelectric ceramic units with controllable curvatures. A new type of Tile transducer for roadway applications was developed in combination with an elastic metal base. Under the action of traffic load, the Tile transducer was subject to both vertical stress and a horizontal tearing force. Laboratory tests were performed on Tile transducers with simply supported and fixed boundary conditions, and the effects of concentrated and uniformly distributed loads on energy harvesting efficiency were analyzed. When the excitation frequency was $6 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and the load was $0 . 7 \mathrm { M P a }$ , the output power of the Plane transducer was $0 . 2 3 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ , while that of the Tile transducer was 24.5 times as large at $5 . 6 5 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ . The ultimate compressive yield strength of a single Tile transducer could reach $2 . 1 8 \ \mathrm { k N }$ , and the load limit was $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { k N }$ at an excitation frequency of $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . This meets traffic load requirements. The open circuit voltage peak did not decrease substantially when 360 000 cyclic loading processes were performed. This indicated that Tile transducer structural performance was stable and that the transducer was durable. Based on the test results, an effective Tile transducer packaging method is proposed for application in road power generation systems.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The world is struggling to develop clean, green, renewable energy because of fossil fuel depletion and growing ecological problems. Ahmad et al.4 gave a detailed review of all potential road energy harvesting methods, including solar, geothermal, piezoelectric, and hybrid systems. The authors also compared various energysaving technologies and considered road energy harvesting materials, practical applications, and commercial status. In recent years, scholars from various countries have performed piezoelectric energy harvesting experiments in the field. Xiong and Wang5 introduced a new piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) and have constructed and installed six prototype PEHs on actual road surfaces. By measuring the output voltage and current under actual traffic movement, it was shown that the electrical productivity of the energy harvester was closely related to the axial shape and size of the vehicle. Song et al.6 designed and optimized a cantilever-type piezoelectric energy harvester, which connected each piezoelectric beam in parallel after rectifying each of the 48 piezoelectric cantilever beams. The collector also performed impedance matching and achieved an output power of $7 3 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ with a power density of $8 . 1 9 \mathrm { \ m W / m } ^ { 2 }$ . Yang et al.7,8 tested the field vehicle response of a stacked piezoelectric energy harvester on the G85 expressway of Zhaotong City, Yunnan province, China. The researchers achieved an open circuit voltage of $2 2 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and successfully lit an LED light plate. Roshani et al.9,10 developed a cylindrical piezoelectric energy harvester consisting of eight cylindrical piezoelectric ceramics $8 \mathrm { m m }$ in diameter sandwiched between two copper plates. When the excitation frequency was $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and the load was $3 \mathrm { k N }$ , the output power was $3 . 6 \mathrm { m W }$ . The transducer structure is important to piezoelectric energy harvesting efficiency. Ibrahim and $\mathrm { \hat { A l i } } ^ { 1 1 }$ reviewed manual and automatic frequency tuning methods for cantilever-type piezoelectric energy harvesters. Several recent tuning strategy developments were discussed and summarized. Erturk et al.12 provided a bistable piezoelectric energy harvester with better output performance and conversion efficiency. Energy conversion was driven by the repulsive force between two permanent magnets, and large periodic oscillations within a wide bandwidth were used to generate sufficient energy. Wang et al.13 designed two detailed stack-structure optimization schemes. The researchers concluded that the two units produced similar output power levels under the same load conditions, but the durability of the U-layer copper foil electrode structure was better than that of the lateral lead electrode structure. Kim et al.14 developed a Cymbal structure that combined two metal caps with piezoelectric ceramic. The Cymbal structure is subjected to both vertical and horizontal stresses, significantly improving piezoelectric ceramic energy output efficiencies. Jasim et al.15 designed a new hierarchically polarized Bridge transducer structure with a large equivalent piezoelectric constant and equivalent capacitance, and performed a forensic analysis of its fatigue failure mode. Previous studies have featured cantilever beam structures with large output energies, but have been limited by difficulty in matching resonant frequencies to the road vibration frequency and achieving device sizes that were suitable for embedding in a pavement structure with strict stiffness and compactness requirements. The stacked structure is compact and easy to manufacture, with a large bearing capacity. However, it is stiff and its output power is small. Although Cymbals and Bridges have large output energies, they are difficult to produce and have unexceptional bearing capacities. Under cyclical fatigue loading, the inner edge of the lower end cap is prone to stress concentration. This leads to the brittle fracture of piezoelectric ceramics. Zhao et al.16 compared the energy harvesting efficiencies of various transducers. Of the various types of transducer structures tested, THUNDER17 and RAINBOW18 transducers from the NASA Langley Research Center offer the largest vibration absorption effects and energy harvesting efficiencies when exposed to low-frequency vibrations. However, the capacity of THUNDER is low and the curvature formed after high-temperature cooling is difficult to predict.19 This makes it unsuitable for road power generation systems. The reported energy harvester data are listed in Table I. Although scholars have performed extensive re-design and optimization of the existing piezoelectric transducer structures, the technology still has difficulty in meeting road power generation specifications. In this paper, ceramic grinding and polishing techniques are used to make curved piezoelectric ceramic units with controllable curvatures. A new type of Tile transducer for roadway applications is then developed in combination with an elastic metal base. The energy output and fatigue characteristics of the Tile transducer are evaluated using laboratory tests and compared to those of Plane transducers manufactured using the same class of process. Laboratory tests are performed under simply supported and fixed boundary conditions, and the effects of concentrated and uniformly distributed loads on energy harvesting efficiency are analyzed. The Tile transducer is then tested to determine its ultimate compressive yield strength and fatigue characteristics. Finally, an effective Tile transducer packaging method is proposed based on the experimental results.

sections.heading: II. TILE TRANSDUCER POWER GENERATION THEORY
sections.text:
The piezoelectric equation is the theoretical basis for piezoelectric energy harvesting technology. The constitutive equations for a linear piezoelectric material under low stress can be written as20

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { S = s ^ { E } T + d _ { t } E , } } \\ { { { } } } \\ { { D = d T + \varepsilon ^ { T } E , } } \end{array}
$$

where $s ^ { E }$ is the flexibility coefficient matrix under a constant electric field, $d _ { t }$ is the transposition of the piezoelectric charge constant matrix, and $\varepsilon ^ { T }$ is the dielectric constant matrix under constant stress.

![](images/d3ebe4dc38c654abe085b4f7b5b625b35f3be23abce47280e3e6f100a1e71fad.jpg)  
FIG. 1. Piezoelectric material vibration modes (a) 33-model and (b) 31-model.

In addition, S is the strain, $E$ is the electric field intensity, $T$ is the stress, $D$ is the electrical displacement, and $d$ is the piezoelectric charge constant matrix.

The mechanical characteristics of the Tile transducer are complex. As shown in Fig. 1, the direction of stress is parallel to that of polarization in the 33-model but perpendicular in the 31-model. The Tile transducer is subject to both vertical stress and a horizontal tearing force, which make it operate according to the 33-model and 31-model simultaneously. Therefore, the equivalent piezoelectric charge constant $d ^ { e f f }$ and equivalent piezoelectric voltage constant $g ^ { e f f }$ of Tile transducer are expressed as follows:14

$$
\begin{array} { r } { { \cal { d } } ^ { e f f } = { d _ { 3 3 } } + { K _ { d } } | { d _ { 3 1 } } | , } \\ { ~ } \\ { { g ^ { e f f } = g _ { 3 3 } + K _ { g } } | { g _ { 3 1 } } | , } \end{array}
$$

where $K _ { d }$ is the comprehensive Tile transducer coefficient for $d _ { 3 3 }$ and $d _ { 3 1 } , K _ { g }$ is the comprehensive Tile transducer coefficient for $g _ { 3 3 }$ and $g _ { 3 1 }$ , and the value depends on the curvature radius of the arched piezoelectric ceramics, the thickness and area of the spring steel sheet, etc.

Under the action of an external force, the open circuit voltage $V$ of the piezoelectric transducer can be expressed as

$$
V = E \cdot t = g ^ { e f f } \frac { t F } { A } = d ^ { e f f } \frac { F } { C _ { P } } ,
$$

where $F$ is the load, $t$ is the piezoelectric material thickness, $A$ is the stressed area of the piezoelectric ceramic, and $C _ { P }$ is the equivalent capacitance.

The charge quantity $Q$ accumulated on the two piezoelectric transducer electrode surfaces can be expressed as

$$
Q = V \cdot C _ { P } = V \varepsilon \varepsilon _ { 0 } \frac { A } { t } = d ^ { e f f } F ,
$$

where $\varepsilon$ is the dielectric constant of the piezoelectric material and $\varepsilon _ { 0 }$ is the vacuum dielectric constant $( 8 . 8 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 2 } \mathrm { F / m } )$ .

The electric power $P$ generated by the piezoelectric transducer can be expressed as

$$
{ \boldsymbol { P } } = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } C { \boldsymbol { P } } ^ { V ^ { 2 } } \cdot { \boldsymbol { f } } = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } { \frac { \left( d ^ { e f f } \right) ^ { 2 } } { \varepsilon \varepsilon _ { 0 } } } \cdot { \boldsymbol { F } } ^ { 2 } \cdot { \frac { t } { A } } \cdot { \boldsymbol { f } } ,
$$

$f$ is the frequency of periodic loading.

sections.heading: A. Transducer fabrication process
sections.text:
A modified piezoelectric ceramic (PZT-506) was used to make Tile transducers. An impedance analyzer (Agilent, E4990A, HIOKL IM3590) was used to measure the piezoelectric characteristics. The geometric dimensions of the Tile and Plane transducers are shown in Table II and the material properties of PZT-506 are shown in Table III. A formula was used to determine the amounts of raw materials to mix and grind finely for pre-sintering. After secondary grinding was complete, a polyvinyl alcohol adhesive was added to the mixture and a cold isostatic press was used to dry-press the mold with a molding pressure of $1 6 \mathrm { M P a }$ . It was then sintered into a block after the glue was discharged. Making a Tile transducer required a grinder and a custom abrasive to produce ceramics with precise curvatures and then polishing their surfaces. The upper and lower surfaces were covered with silver electrodes and subjected to a polarization treatment. The side electrode was designed to account for the fact that the upper and lower piezoelectric ceramic surfaces must be bonded to aluminum and spring steel sheets, respectively. The silver electrodes on the upper and lower piezoelectric ceramic surfaces were extended to the side via the silver coating method to form positive and negative electrode wire welding. The Tile and Plane transducers were from the same sintered ceramic batch with a volume of $3 2 0 0 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ . TABLE II. Geometric dimensions of the Tile and Plane transducers.

The metal base was made from $6 5 \mathrm { { M n } }$ spring steel. The curvature of the spring steel corresponded to that of the piezoelectric ceramic. The projection length was $7 0 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , the width was $2 2 \mathrm { ~ m m }$ , and the thickness was $2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ . The critical performance requirements for the spring steel sheet were a high elastic limit, yield strength, and toughness. Only the tempered troostite structure offered the required properties. Therefore, the hot coil method was used to make the steel sheet. The plane spring steel sheet was put into a surface mold with a curvature of 1/200.5 while still hot and rolled to form a surface. Next, the curved spring steel plate was quenched at ${ 8 1 0 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ oil cooled, and then tempered at $3 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ The upper cover sheet was made from pure aluminum, the surface area was consistent with that of the ceramic, and the thickness was $0 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ . The aluminum sheet served to protect the piezoelectric ceramics. Finally, the piezoelectric ceramic, metal base, and aluminum sheet surfaces were cleaned with alcohol and then bonded with E-51 epoxy insulating adhesive. The epoxy resin layer on both sides of the spring steel sheet was thickened to enhance adhesion between the layer and the spring steel sheet. The completed Tile transducer is shown in Fig. 2.

sections.heading: C. Determination of the test force and test frequency
sections.text:
Zhao et al.16 assumed that freeway vehicles traveled at $1 0 0 \mathrm { k m / h }$ and had $4 . 5 \mathrm { ~ m ~ }$ wheelbases. The researchers also assumed that the traffic volume in each lane was 2000 vehicles per h. This generated time intervals between axles and vehicles of $0 . 1 6 2 \ s$ and $1 . 8 \ s ,$ respectively. Thus, the traffic load frequency was $0 . 1 \mathrm { H z } { - } 1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . After comprehensive consideration, the excitation frequencies tested were $2 \mathrm { H z } ,$ , 4 Hz, 6 Hz, $8 \ : \mathrm { H z } ,$ , and $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . For small cars, the load on a single tire is typically between $0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { M P a }$ and $0 . 2 6 ~ \mathrm { M P a }$ , and a typical axle load is $0 . 7 \ \mathrm { M P a }$ . Given the range of vehicle stresses, the stresses applied to the Tile and Plane transducers were assumed to include $0 . 2 \mathrm { M P a } , 0 . 2 6 \mathrm { M P a } , 0 . 3 7 5 \mathrm { M P a } ,$ $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { M P a } ,$ , and $0 . 7 \ \mathrm { M P a }$ . The area of each piezoelectric ceramic was $0 . 0 0 0 8 \ \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ . As shown in Table IV, the Tile transducer was tested experimentally under three loading conditions: Tile1 had a simply supported boundary and was bound only in the horizontal direction, while Tile2 and Tile3 were encapsulated with E-51 epoxy and bound in both the horizontal and vertical directions. The Computer Number Control was used to sculpt a white top with the same curvature as the Tile3 transducer. Therefore, Tile1 and Tile2 were subject to concentrated loads, while Tile3 was encapsulated in a $4 \mathrm { m m }$ -thick slab of the same curvature and subject to a uniformly distributed load. sections.heading: A. Open circuit voltage
sections.text:
Figure 5(a) shows that the transducer open circuit voltage increases with the excitation frequency within the $2 \ \mathrm { H z } { - } 6 \ \mathrm { H z }$ frequency range. The voltage continues to increase within the $6 \ \mathrm { H z } \mathrm { - } 1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ frequency range, but the rate of this increase is slower. This is consistent with the conclusion reached by Yang et al.21 The equivalent piezoelectric charge circuit is shown in Fig. 4, where $C _ { P }$ is the equivalent capacitance of the piezoelectric transducer, $R _ { L }$ is the leakage resistance plus the load, and $V$ is the open circuit voltage.

![](images/d83e4a43a0428944ac26166369202317c4f70e58098950ee8f2b8371f55943fd.jpg)

Equation (8) can be obtained using Kirchhoff’s current law,

$$
i _ { 0 } = i _ { C } + i _ { R } ,
$$

where $i _ { 0 }$ is the piezoelectric induced current, $i _ { C }$ is the capacitor charging current, and $i _ { R }$ is the output current.

Under the action of dynamic load, the piezoelectric transducer generates a charge $Q ,$ part of which is stored in the equivalent capacitor $C _ { i }$ , and the other part is dissipated by $R _ { L }$ due to leakage resistance. A lower excitation frequency leads to slower charge storage, more charge dissipation through $R _ { L }$ and thus a lower open circuit voltage across the equivalent capacitance.

Figure 5(b) shows that the open circuit voltage of the Plane transducer is linear with the load. The planar piezoelectric ceramic is theoretically a linear material. The charge density should be proportional to the external force, as confirmed by the laboratory test data. It is worth noting that the Tile transducer open circuit voltage is linear with the load indicating the existence of an equivalent piezoelectric voltage constant $g ^ { e f f }$ .

The open circuit voltage of the Tile2 transducer is $1 7 \%$ smaller than that of the Tile1 transducer. This demonstrates that the energy harvesting efficiency of the Tile transducer with simply supported boundaries is higher than that of the unit with fixed boundaries. This is because the power generation efficiency of the Tile transducer depends on the size of the vibration space. Therefore, the reduction in energy harvesting efficiency provided upon encapsulating the boundary depends on the spring steel sheet length fixed by the epoxy resin, which can be reduced by increasing the spring steel sheet length. The open circuit voltage of the Tile3 transducer is $2 6 \%$ smaller than that of the Tile2 transducer, which demonstrates that the Tile transducer energy harvesting efficiency is higher under a concentrated load than under a uniform load. This provides useful information for Tile transducer packaging design. When the excitation frequency is $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and the load is $0 . 7 \mathrm { M P a }$ , the open circuit voltage of the Plane transducer is $4 6 \mathrm { V }$ , while that of the Tile1 transducer is 4.8 times higher at $2 2 2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ . According to Eq. (5), the Tile transducer equivalent piezoelectric constant s geff and $d ^ { e f f }$ are 4.8 times those of the Plane transducer.

sections.heading: B. Short circuit current
sections.text:
Figure 6(a) shows that the current increases significantly with the excitation frequency. It can be seen from Fig. 6(b) that the short circuit current is linear with the change in load. This is consistent with the law demonstrated by the open circuit voltage and provides further evidence of the existence of an equivalent piezoelectric charge constant $d ^ { e f f }$ for the Tile transducer.

The short circuit current of the Tile2 transducer is $1 6 \%$ lower than that of the Tile1 transducer. This demonstrates that the energy harvesting efficiency of the Tile transducer with a simply supported boundary is higher than that of a unit with a fixed boundary. The short circuit current of the Tile3 transducer is $3 2 \%$ smaller than that of the Tile2 transducer because the Tile transducer energy harvesting efficiency is higher under a concentrated load than under a uniform load. When the excitation frequency is $1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and the load is $0 . 7 \mathrm { M P a }$ , the short circuit current of the Plane transducer is $2 0 \mu \mathrm { A }$ , while that of the Tile1 transducer is 5 times higher at $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { A }$ . This is consistent with the open circuit voltage results.

sections.heading: C. Output power under various load resistances
sections.text:
As shown in Fig. 7(a), when the excitation frequency is $6 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and the load is $0 . 7 \mathrm { M P a }$ , the load voltages of the Tile and Plane transducers increase with the load resistance. The trend of this change is significant in early stages, but stabilizes later. When the increase in the load resistance $R _ { 0 }$ is infinite, the output voltage is infinitesimally close to the open circuit voltage.

Equation (9) is used to calculate the output power under various load resistances. As shown in Fig. 7(b), the output power increases with the load until it reaches a maximum and then decreases. The Tile1, Tile2, Tile3, and Plane transducers reach their maximum output power levels at optimal loads22 of $3 . 2 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ $3 . 4 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ , $3 . 8 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ , and $3 . 8 \mathrm { M } \Omega$ , respectively. The optimal load resistance of the Tile transducer is smaller than that of the Plane transducer. This aids the energy harvesting efficiency of the former. At the optimal load resistance, the output power of the Plane transducer is $0 . 2 3 ~ \mathrm { m W } _ { : }$ , while that of the Tile1 transducer is 24.5 times higher at $5 . 6 5 \mathrm { m W }$ ,

$$
{ \cal P } _ { 0 } = \frac { { U _ { 0 } } ^ { 2 } } { R _ { 0 } } ,
$$

where $P _ { 0 }$ is the output power, $U _ { 0 }$ is the output voltage, and $R _ { 0 }$ is the load resistance.

The optimal load resistance of the Tile2 transducer was tested under various loads and frequencies. As shown in the inset of Fig. 8(a), when the load is $0 . 7 \ \mathrm { \ M P a }$ , the excitation frequency is in the range of $1 \ \mathrm { H z } \mathrm { - } 1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The optimal load resistance of the Tile2 transducer decreases nonlinearly as the excitation frequency increases. The decreasing trend starts out fast but stabilizes resembling a power function curve. The optimal load resistance expression of the Tile2 transducer is obtained via nonlinear regression of optimal load resistances at various excitation frequencies,

As shown in the inset of Fig. 8(b), when the excitation frequency is $6 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , the optimal load resistance of the Tile2 transducer does not change with the load. This demonstrates that the optimal load resistance of the Tile transducer has little relation to the load.

sections.heading: D. Compressive yield strength and fatigue tests
sections.text:
As shown in Fig. 9, the compressive yield strength of the Tile2 transducer was tested using a WAW-1000 universal testing machine with a loading speed of $5 0 \mathrm { N } / s$ . During loading, the Tile transducer was damaged due to a large displacement caused by a broken plastic engineering base. An aluminum base could be used in the packaging process instead. As shown in Figs. 10(a) and 10(b), the limiting value of the compressive yield strength of the Tile2 transducer is $2 . 1 8 \ \mathrm { k N }$ and the displacement limit is $0 . 6 1 4 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ . The Tile2 transducer can be protected by including a $0 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ gap in the packaging design.

![](images/d6f368662b89b6f38d128a10e55f0802a832c4b03e3f3738d4aefe74c8107900.jpg)  
FIG. 9. Compressive yield strength test.

The load limit of the Tile transducer under low frequency vibration was tested using a fatigue-testing machine. The experiment continued until the Tile transducer broke. The excitation frequency is $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . The experiment starts with a load of $1 0 0 \mathrm { N }$ and an additional $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { N }$ is loaded per stage, and the loading time is $3 0 0 ~ \mathsf { s }$ . When the excitation frequency is $1 0 \mathrm { H z } ,$ the load limit of the Tile1 transducer is $1 \mathrm { k N }$ . After fixing the spring steel sheet boundary with epoxy resin, the load limit of the Tile2 transducer is $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { k N }$ . Both of these are much larger than the $4 5 \mathrm { N }$ load limit of the THUNDER transducer.17 This makes Tile transducers applicable to road power generation systems.

The fatigue characteristics of the Tile2 transducer were tested using a fatigue-testing machine. The Tile2 transducer was subjected to 360 000 loading cycles with an excitation frequency of $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and load of $0 . 7 \ \mathrm { M P a }$ . The open circuit voltage was recorded every 20 000 cycles. As shown in Figs. 11(a) and 11(b), the open circuit voltage peak decreases by $2 . 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ . This is due to the normal soft piezoelectric ceramic depolarization phenomenon. In addition, the epoxy resin layer at the bond between the piezoelectric ceramic and spring steel sheet shows no signs of shedding, which demonstrates that the Tile transducer offers stable, long-lasting structural properties.

sections.heading: E. Packaging design
sections.text:
Figure 12 shows an effective Tile transducer packaging method proposed based on the test results. The key design elements are:

(1) According to the results of the load distribution test, the efficiency was higher under a concentrated load than under a uniform load. Thus, a concentrated load is applied to the Tile transducer by bolting the upper cover plate to the bar-shaped force transfer rod.   
(2) According to the results of the boundary condition test, the energy harvesting efficiency of the Tile transducer with simply supported boundaries was higher than that of the Tile transducer with fixed boundaries. Thus, the transducer slot in the bottom plate is used to improve the free vibration space of the transducer instead of fixing the Tile transducer with epoxy resin.   
(3) According to the results of the compressive yield strength test, the limit value of the displacement limit is $0 . 6 1 4 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ . Thus,

(4) According to the results of the short circuit current test, the current of a single Tile transducer reaches $1 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { A }$ at $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $0 . 7 \ \mathrm { M P a }$ . The piezoelectric transducers are rectified and connected in parallel, which increases the current of the piezoelectric energy harvester to the milliampere level.

(5) According to the output power test results, the number of Tile transducers can be increased in the depth direction using a multi-layered dowel steel. This increases the output power of the piezoelectric energy harvester.

sections.heading: V. CONCLUSION
sections.text:
Practical engineering applications for road piezoelectric power generation and piezoelectric transducer structures were reviewed. Existing piezoelectric transducer structures have difficulty meeting road power generation requirements. Therefore, a new type of roadbased Tile transducer was developed. The Tile transducer offers a high equivalent piezoelectric constant, remarkable energy output, compact structure, high bearing capacity, and easy manufacturability. Analysis of the experimental data allows us to draw the following conclusions:

(1) The optimal output power can be obtained by applying a concentrated load to a Tile transducer under simply supported boundary conditions. When the excitation frequency was $6 \mathrm { H z }$ and the load was $0 . 7 \mathrm { M P a }$ , the output power levels of Tile1, Tile2, and Tile3 were $5 . 6 5 \mathrm { m W }$ , $3 . 0 3 \mathrm { m W }$ , and $1 . 8 1 \mathrm { m W } _ { : }$ , respectively.

(2) Compared to Cantilever, Stacked, Cylindrical, and Bridge transducer structures, the Tile transducer has compact structure and high output power. When the excitation frequency was $6 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and the load was $0 . 7 \ \mathrm { M P a }$ , the output power of the Plane transducer was $0 . 2 3 \mathrm { m W }$ , while that of Tile1 was as large as $5 . 6 5 \mathrm { m W }$ . The output power density of Tile1 reached $4 . 0 \dot { 4 } \ \mathrm { W / m } ^ { 2 }$ , which is substantially higher than any of the power densities listed in Table I.

(3) The Tile transducer exhibited more stable and durable structural performance than the Cymbal, Bridge, and THUNDER transducer structures. The compressive yield strength of a single Tile transducer could reach $2 . 1 8 \ \mathrm { k N }$ , and the load limit value at an excitation frequency of $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ was $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { k N }$ . The Tile transducer was subjected to 360 000 loading cycles at an excitation frequency of $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and load of $0 . 7 \ \mathrm { M P a }$ without reducing its peak open circuit voltage.

(4) A Tile transducer with a thickness of $4 \ \mathrm { m m }$ has a larger equivalent internal resistance and smaller output current. In order to reduce the transducer matching impedance and increase the output power, a U-shaped interlayer copper foil electrode should be used to stack $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ -thick arch piezoelectric ceramics. Then, an integrated piezoelectric energy harvester can be used to perform field experiments on the roadway.
